lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Antisthenes, Crates — we've got nothing on. Why don't we take a walk over to the entrance and have a look at the new arrivals coming down? See what sort they are, and what each of them is up to.

lines.speaker: Antisthenes
lines.text: Let's go, Diogenes. It ought to be a pleasant spectacle — some of them weeping, some begging to be let off, a few barely managing to come down at all, with Hermes shoving them by the neck while they brace their heels and lean backward for no good reason.

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: Well, while we're at it, let me tell you what I saw on my own way down.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Tell us, Crates. Sounds like you witnessed something thoroughly ridiculous.

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: A whole crowd came down with me, but the notable ones were Ismenodorus — our local rich man — and Arsaces, the satrap of Media, and Oroetes the Armenian. Now Ismenodorus had been murdered by bandits up near Cithaeron — on his way to Eleusis, I think — and he was groaning, clutching his wound with both hands, calling out the names of his babies (he'd left them as newborns), and reproaching himself for his recklessness: he'd crossed Cithaeron and travelled through the country around Eleutherae — completely deserted because of the wars — with only two slaves in his train. And he was carrying five gold cups and four drinking-bowls on him.

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: Arsaces, on the other hand — elderly by now, and, I have to say, rather impressive-looking — was carrying on in the full barbarian style, indignant at having to walk on foot, demanding that someone bring up his horse. Because the horse had died along with him: both of them run through with a single thrust by some Thracian peltast, in the skirmish on the Araxes against the Cappadocian. Arsaces, the way he told it, had charged out well ahead of the rest. The Thracian stood his ground, ducked under his shield, knocked aside Arsaces' lance, then planted his pike and skewered both man and horse.

lines.speaker: Antisthenes
lines.text: How was that even possible, Crates? Both of them, one blow?

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: Easily, Antisthenes. Arsaces was charging in with a twenty-cubit lance held out in front. The Thracian deflected the strike with his shield, the point went past him, and he dropped to one knee and received the charge on his pike — wounding the horse under the breastbone, which impaled itself on the weapon by sheer momentum and rage. And Arsaces was driven straight through, from the groin clear out the backside. So you see what happened — the horse did most of the work, really, not the man. But there he was, indignant at being treated like everyone else, demanding to come down as a cavalryman.

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: Then there was Oroetes — utterly tender-footed, couldn't even stand on the ground, let alone walk. It's something all the Medes do, when they get off their horses: they pick their way on tiptoe as if they were stepping on thorns. So when he threw himself down and lay there refusing by any means to get up, our good Hermes hoisted him up and carried him all the way to the ferry. [laughs] I was watching.

lines.speaker: Antisthenes
lines.text: When I came down, I didn't mix in with the rest. I left them to their wailing, ran ahead to the ferry, and bagged a spot — somewhere I could have a comfortable crossing. And during the trip, while they were weeping and being seasick, I had a thoroughly enjoyable time at their expense.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Well, you two got those for travelling companions. I had Blepsias the moneylender from Pisa, and Lampis the Acarnanian — a mercenary captain — and Damis the rich man from Corinth. Damis had been poisoned by his son. Lampis had cut his own throat over his love for the courtesan Myrtium. And Blepsias, the wretch, was said to have wasted away from hunger — and you could see it: pale beyond belief, thin to the last possible degree. So even though I knew, I asked them how they'd died. To Damis, when he started blaming his son, I said: 'It's not as if you didn't deserve it. You had a thousand talents, you lived in luxury at ninety, and you gave your eighteen-year-old boy four obols a day.' And you, Acarnanian — he was groaning too, cursing Myrtium — 'Why are you blaming Eros? Blame yourself. You never flinched from an enemy in your life — you charged ahead of everyone, you loved danger — and then some random little tart, with a few fake tears and theatrical sighs, brought down the great hero.' As for Blepsias, he was already accusing himself, ahead of me — going on about his enormous stupidity, hoarding money for heirs who weren't even relatives, thinking he'd live forever, the fool. Anyway, their groaning provided me with no small amusement at the time.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: But here we are at the entrance. We should keep a lookout — watch the arrivals from a distance. [pause] Good grief. So many, and all sorts, and every one of them weeping — except for these newborns and infants. But even the really ancient ones are lamenting. What's this? Has the love of life got such a hold on them?

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: I want to ask this very old man. — You there. Why are you weeping, at your age, now that you're dead? Why so indignant, my good fellow — and an old man at that? Were you a king, perhaps?

lines.speaker: The Old Pauper
lines.text: Not at all.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: A satrap, then?

lines.speaker: The Old Pauper
lines.text: No, not that either.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Were you rich, then? Does it pain you to have died and left behind a life of luxury?

lines.speaker: The Old Pauper
lines.text: Nothing of the sort. I was about ninety years old. I scraped a bare living from a rod and line — utterly destitute, childless, lame on top of it, and going blind.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: [pause] And — being all that — you still wanted to live?

lines.speaker: The Old Pauper
lines.text: Yes. The light was sweet, and to be dead was a terrible thing, and to be avoided.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: You're out of your mind, old man — playing the schoolboy with necessity, and you the same age as the ferryman. What's there left to say about the young, when men of his years are this in love with life? They ought to be chasing death down as a cure for the miseries of old age. — Anyway, let's move along, before someone spots us loitering here at the entrance and suspects we're planning to make a run for it.
